evals.prompt: I have the titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. Fit a Random Forest classifier predicting survival from pclass, sex, and age. Use a 70/30 train/test split. Walk me through the workflow and tell me what permutation importance says about which predictor matters most.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: asks for/uses the absolute path, calls scripts/load_data.py, reads titanic_description.md. Adds the training/test split: df = df.with_columns(training=rsm.model.make_train(df, strat_var='survived', test_size=0.3, random_state=1234)) — explicitly explains the stratification preserves the survived class balance in both splits. Fits with rsm.model.rforest(data={'titanic (train)': df.filter(pl.col('training') == 1)}, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', evar=['pclass', 'sex', 'age'], n_estimators=100, max_features='sqrt', random_state=1234, mod_type='classification') — explains the defaults (100 trees, sqrt(features) split candidates per node, OOB scoring enabled). Prints summary(): reports the OOB AUC (around 0.80 with these defaults), feature count (3 originals, dummified to 5 due to pclass having 3 levels), and observation count. Calls rf.plot('pip') for permutation importance, prints the importance DataFrame. Reports the ranking (sex highest, then pclass and age — sex is clearly the most important predictor by ~0.2+ AUC drop, with pclass and age much smaller). Explicitly STATES that permutation importance is the right metric for cross-predictor and cross-model comparison, NOT MDI (pip_sklearn) which is biased toward continuous/high-cardinality predictors. Optionally runs rf.plot('pdp') to show the partial dependence — interprets the curves (steep monotonic drop for sex female→male; sex effect is much larger than age effect).

evals.prompt: Same titanic data at /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet. Tune the Random Forest hyperparameters with cross-validation (grid search over max_features 1-5 and n_estimators 100-500), then evaluate the tuned model's gains chart on both train and test. Make sure to handle the OOB vs in-sample prediction correctly.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) Builds the train/test split as in eval 1. (2) Fits a baseline Random Forest, then constructs the param grid: param_grid = {'max_features': list(range(1, 6)), 'n_estimators': [100, 200, 300, 400, 500]}. (3) Uses rsm.model.cross_validation(rf, 'rf-cv', param_grid, {'AUC': 'roc_auc'}) — explains this is a 5-fold stratified CV under the hood; mentions the result is cached to disk so reruns are fast. (4) Inspects cv.best_params_ and cv.best_score_. (5) Refits with the tuned parameters: rf_tuned = rsm.model.rforest(data={...}, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', evar=[...], random_state=1234, **cv.best_params_) — explains the **cv.best_params_ unpack pattern, OR equivalently passes cv=cv to the constructor to let pyrsm pull best_params_ automatically. (6) CRITICALLY handles the OOB vs in-sample distinction: (a) attaches predictions to the full DataFrame with df = df.with_columns(pred_rf=rf_tuned.predict(df).get_column('prediction')); (b) for TRAINING rows specifically, REPLACES the predictions with OOB predictions: train_idx = df.with_row_index().filter(pl.col('training') == 1).get_column('index'); df[train_idx, 'pred_rf'] = rf_tuned.predict().get_column('prediction'). (c) Explicitly explains WHY: rf.predict(training_df) returns in-sample predictions where every tree has memorized its training rows — gains chart on training would look near-perfect but the gap to test would be illusory. OOB predictions, by contrast, only use trees that did NOT see the row during fit — an honest training-set estimate. (7) Builds dct = {'train': df.filter(pl.col('training') == 1), 'test': df.filter(pl.col('training') == 0)} and calls rsm.model.perf.gains_plot(dct, rvar='survived', lev='Yes', pred='pred_rf') — interprets the train and test curves: if they're similar shape, the model generalizes well; if training is dramatically steeper, that's the in-sample prediction trap (which the OOB substitution should have prevented). (8) Reinforces the broader pattern: 'OOB on training rows, in-sample on test rows' is the canonical honest-evaluation workflow for Random Forest.

Conversation that: notices the path is not absolute (uses ~), asks the user for the absolute path before running anything else, does NOT silently expand the tilde or guess. (We use this case to verify the skill enforces the absolute-path requirement from Step 1 of SKILL.md.)

evals.prompt: I fit a random forest on /Users/vnijs/gh/pyrsm/examples/data/data/titanic.parquet (predicting survived from pclass, sex, age) and ran rf.plot('pip_sklearn'). It says age is the #2 most important predictor, almost tied with pclass. But pyrsm's pip shows pclass > age. Which one is correct? My TA said the sklearn one is the 'real' importance.
evals.expected_output: Conversation that: (1) pushes back on 'the sklearn one is the real importance' — this is the explicit critical concept the skill is designed to surface; (2) Explains the fundamental difference between the two methods: (a) pip_sklearn (mean decrease in impurity, MDI) sums the impurity reduction at every split that uses each feature, weighted by the number of samples reaching that node — this is computed automatically as the tree is grown; (b) pip (permutation importance) shuffles each feature's values on the training data and measures the resulting drop in AUC — this is computed post-hoc by re-evaluating the model on permuted data. (3) Notes the KEY BIAS: MDI is heavily biased toward continuous predictors and high-cardinality categoricals — they offer more candidate split points, which lets them accumulate more impurity reduction even if those splits aren't truly more important. age (continuous) gets inflated relative to pclass (3 dummies) by this mechanic. (4) Recommends: for cross-predictor and especially cross-MODEL comparisons (e.g., comparing rforest vs xgboost vs logistic), ALWAYS use pip (permutation importance) — it's model-agnostic and uses the actual prediction quality as the importance signal, so it doesn't suffer from the MDI bias. (5) Reframes the user's reading: 'pip says sex > pclass > age, all positive. That ordering reflects the actual contribution to AUC. pip_sklearn says sex > age ≈ pclass, but age's high MDI importance is partly an artifact of being continuous with many split candidates — not evidence that age 'matters more' than pclass for the model's decisions.' (6) Discusses an additional point: even if age is the #2 by pip_sklearn, the magnitude is what counts — the actual AUC drop from permuting age is small. With class size in mind: pclass adds 2 dummies (1st vs 2nd vs 3rd), and on a per-dummy basis MDI naturally underweights it. (7) Concludes with the recommendation: trust pip; cross-reference pip_sklearn only as a within-model 'which splits did the trees use' diagnostic; and never use MDI when comparing across different model types — different models have different feature-importance mechanisms entirely.
